title: What Happens to Your Fingers in the Bath?
description:
Send this to the friend who stays in the bath until they're a raisin.
Fingers wrinkle because the autonomic nervous system narrows blood vessels under the skin (Newcastle University), and fingers that lost their nerve supply stay smooth (Clinical Autonomic Research, 2006). A 2025 Binghamton study found the wrinkles come back in the same pattern every time. Pruney skin when you haven't been in water? Cleveland Clinic says talk to a doctor.

structure_note: A clue trail: three clues (the grip study, the same-pattern-every-time study, the vessels that never move) lead to the culprit. Frame 1 is a close-up of a pruned hand lifting out of bath water with a duck and a '5 MIN' kitchen timer on the tub edge and the A/B pills. Then the soap bar shooting out of the hero's grip (relatable), a marble race (wrinkly vs smooth hand, '+12%' tag) with tire-tread overlay and a small grey 'other study: no difference' stamp, the re-hook: a fingertip 'scan' of day 1 vs day 2 overlaid and matching line for line, an x-ray-cyan zoom into the fingertip showing fixed blood vessels, then a nerve lighting up, the vessels narrowing and the skin folding (pill B checked), a smooth finger with a cut nerve icon next to a wrinkled one, the side-stitch tease, and the hand sinking back into the frame-1 water. Different from sitting (dose guess, office), doorway (lab yes/no), funny bone (anatomy tour) and stand-up (direction guess): no body-map, no yes/no, no dose; a detective clue trail.
safety: Calm, curious-friend tone, no medical advice. The grip benefit is framed as 'one study' with 'not every study agrees' (Haseleu 2014 PLoS One found none). The cut-nerve fact comes from peer-reviewed clinical studies (replanted fingers, wrinkle test); visuals schematic only, no injury or amputation images (show a 'cut nerve' as an icon, not a wound). The description carries Cleveland Clinic's 'pruney without water, talk to a doctor' note. Bath scene: hero's hand and a tub, no nudity.
